name: Card testing
plainEnglish: A criminal who has a card number makes tiny payments to find out whether the card works before using it for something bigger.
signs: Several very small payments in a few minutes
Online merchants the customer has never used
Refused attempts with a wrong security code or expiry date
The same merchant charging many different cards the same small amount
howToRespond: Decline, block the card and send the customer a replacement.

name: Account takeover
plainEnglish: A criminal gets into a real customer's account and uses it as if they were the customer.
signs: A device or browser the customer has never used before
Password, email or phone number changed shortly before a payment
A new payee followed quickly by a large payment
Someone else controlling the customer's device remotely
Payments sized just under a limit that triggers extra checks
howToRespond: Stop the payment and contact the customer on details held before the recent changes.

name: SIM swap
plainEnglish: A criminal takes over the customer's mobile number, so security codes sent by text message go to the criminal instead.
signs: The mobile network reports a recent SIM change or number transfer
A password reset or new device approved by text message code soon after
The customer says their phone has suddenly lost all signal
The real customer can only be reached by another channel, such as email
howToRespond: Stop the payment. Do not rely on text message codes; verify the customer another way.

name: Money mule
plainEnglish: An account is used to receive stolen money and pass it on, hiding where it came from. The account holder may be recruited with the promise of easy pay.
signs: Money arrives from strangers and leaves again almost immediately
Activity far above what the customer's income would explain
A quiet account that suddenly becomes busy
The customer describes a 'job' that involves moving money and keeping a cut
howToRespond: Hold the outgoing payment and review the source of the incoming funds.

name: Synthetic identity
plainEnglish: An account opened in the name of a person who does not really exist, built from a mix of real and invented details, usually to obtain credit that will never be repaid.
signs: Identity details that match no record older than the account
An address, device or network shared with many other applicants
No everyday life on the account: no salary, bills or routine spending
A sudden run of maximum-value credit purchases
The customer cannot be reached by phone
howToRespond: Decline and refer the account for an identity review.

name: Friendly fraud (chargeback abuse)
plainEnglish: A real customer makes a real purchase, receives it, and then falsely claims they did not make it or never received it in order to get a refund.
signs: The purchase came from the customer's own usual device and location
Proof of delivery or use: signed for, boarded, reviewed
A history of similar claims
The customer was in contact with the merchant about the order
howToRespond: Reject the claim and share the evidence with the customer.

name: Authorised push payment scam
plainEnglish: A genuine customer is tricked into sending their own money to a criminal. The customer makes the payment themselves and often insists that it is fine.
signs: The customer has been told what to say, or told the bank may ask questions
Pressure, secrecy or urgency coming from a third party
The name typed does not match the name on the receiving account
The customer is on a long phone call or sharing their screen while paying
Payments that keep rising to someone the customer has never met
Bank details for a known supplier changed by email
howToRespond: Stop the payment and talk to the customer away from the scammer's influence. A customer saying 'it's fine' is not enough.

name: Promo and bonus abuse
plainEnglish: One person opens many accounts to collect sign-up or referral bonuses that are meant to be claimed once.
signs: Many accounts opened from one device
Accounts sharing an address, bank account or near-identical emails
Each account does the minimum to earn the bonus and nothing else
Bonus withdrawn as soon as it lands
howToRespond: Decline the payout and link the accounts for review.

name: Crypto cash-out to a fresh wallet
plainEnglish: Stolen or fraudulent funds are converted to crypto and sent to a brand-new wallet, where they are very hard to recover.
signs: A new account, or a new device on an old account, just before the withdrawal
Security settings weakened shortly before the withdrawal
Nearly the whole balance leaving at once
Destination wallet created very recently or linked to risky wallets
howToRespond: Hold the withdrawal and review how the funds and the login got there before anything leaves.

name: Genuine customer: travelling abroad
plainEnglish: A real customer spending in another country. A foreign location on its own is not fraud.
signs: The customer's own card, PIN or trusted device was used
Spending that fits a trip: hotels, transport, food
Earlier travel bookings on the account
No recent changes to login or contact details
howToRespond: Approve. Declining leaves a real customer stranded without money abroad.

name: Genuine customer: big one-off purchase
plainEnglish: A real customer making an unusually large payment for something planned. A high amount on its own is not fraud.
signs: Earlier deposit or dealings with the same business
The name typed matches a long-established business account
The customer checked the details themselves, through a trusted route
Usual device, and nobody else on a call or sharing the screen
howToRespond: Approve. Blocking a planned purchase is frustrating and can cost the customer their order.

name: Genuine customer: new phone
plainEnglish: A real customer who has replaced their phone. A new device matters most when other warning signs come with it.
signs: The new device passed a strong identity check, such as a face match
No SIM change reported by the mobile network
Payment fits the customer's routine or goes to a long-standing payee
The customer can explain it naturally
howToRespond: Approve. Look for a new device combined with other changes before treating it as a takeover.

name: Genuine customer: paying someone new
plainEnglish: A real customer paying a new person or business for an ordinary reason. Urgency or a short temper alone does not make it a scam.
signs: The name typed matches the name on the receiving account
The receiving account is long-established
The customer got the details first-hand and was not told what to say
Nobody is on a call with the customer while they pay
howToRespond: Approve. Compare with a scam: here the customer chose the payee and verified it themselves.

name: Genuine customer: money in, money out
plainEnglish: Money arriving and leaving quickly for an innocent reason, such as collecting friends' shares for a booking or moving the proceeds of a sale.
signs: Senders are people the customer already knows and has dealt with
A clear real-world reason that matches the account's history
Money goes to a known business or the customer's own account
The customer keeps no 'commission'
howToRespond: Approve. Mule activity involves strangers, vague stories and a cut for the account holder.

name: Genuine customer: brand-new account
plainEnglish: A real person who has only just opened an account, such as a student or someone who has recently moved for work. A short history is not the same as a fake identity.
signs: Identity confirmed with official documents and a live face check
Income from a recognisable source, such as an employer or student lender
One device used only for this account
Spending that looks like real life: rent, food, travel
howToRespond: Approve. Synthetic identities lack real-life activity and share details with other accounts.

name: Genuine customer: valid refund claim
plainEnglish: A real customer who really was charged in error or by a fraudster and is asking for their money back.
signs: The disputed payment came from a device or place never linked to the customer
The customer acted quickly, for example by freezing their card
Few or no previous claims
Records support the customer's account of what happened
howToRespond: Approve the refund. Rejecting a valid claim leaves a fraud victim out of pocket.

name: Genuine customer: real referrals
plainEnglish: A real customer who recommended the service to real people and earned the bonuses fairly.
signs: Each referred person has their own device and address
Referred accounts are used for everyday spending
A modest number of referrals over a sensible period

name: Genuine customer: crypto to their own wallet
plainEnglish: A real customer moving their own crypto to a wallet they control. A new wallet is not automatically a risky one.
signs: A long trading history on the account
No changes to security settings, and strong login checks passed
A small test payment sent first, or a wallet used many times before
No remote access, no one coaching the customer, no links to risky wallets
howToRespond: Approve. Compare with a scam: the customer set the wallet up themselves and nobody else is involved.

name: Genuine customer: lots of small payments
plainEnglish: A real customer making many small payments for an everyday reason, such as commuting, in-game purchases or a fuel pump check.
signs: Payments made in person or approved in the customer's own app
One familiar merchant the customer has used for a long time
A routine that repeats week after week
No refused attempts
howToRespond: Approve. Card testing involves unfamiliar merchants, typed-in card details and refused attempts.
